Company Leave Policy — Introduction: This policy defines the paid and unpaid leave entitlements available to all full-time and part-time employees of the company. Every employee is expected to familiarise themselves with these provisions, which are administered by the People Operations team and reviewed annually by executive leadership.

Annual Leave Entitlement: Full-time employees accrue twenty (20) days of paid annual leave per calendar year, credited at a rate of 1.67 days per completed month of service. Employees may carry over a maximum of five (5) unused annual leave days into the following year; any balance above this limit is forfeited on 31 December. Annual leave requests must be submitted through the HR portal at least ten (10) business days in advance and are approved subject to operational requirements.

Sick Leave Entitlement: Employees are entitled to twelve (12) days of paid sick leave per calendar year. Sick leave of up to two (2) consecutive days requires only manager notification, whereas absences of three (3) or more consecutive days require a medical certificate issued by a registered practitioner. Unused sick leave does not carry over and is not paid out upon termination of employment.

Parental and Family Leave: Eligible employees who have completed twelve (12) months of continuous service are entitled to sixteen (16) weeks of paid parental leave following the birth or adoption of a child. Parental leave may be taken by either parent and can be shared between both parents. Employees must notify their manager at least four (4) weeks before the intended start date.

Public Holidays and Approval Process: The company observes all gazetted public holidays, and employees required to work on a public holiday receive a compensatory day off. All leave requests are recorded in the central leave management system, and managers are responsible for ensuring adequate team coverage before approving any request. Disputes regarding leave approval are escalated to the HR Business Partner for resolution.

Unpaid and Special Leave: Where an employee has exhausted their paid entitlements, they may request unpaid leave of up to thirty (30) days per year with manager and HR approval. Special leave provisions exist for bereavement, jury duty, and emergency volunteering, for which up to five (5) additional paid days may be granted at the discretion of the Head of People Operations.

Subscription and Billing Policy — Overview: This policy governs how customers are billed for access to the platform, including trial periods, renewal behaviour, payment methods, cancellation, and refunds. The policy applies to all self-service and enterprise subscription plans unless superseded by a negotiated master services agreement.

Free Trial Period: New customers receive a thirty (30) day free trial beginning on the date of account activation. During the trial, customers have access to the full feature set of the selected plan. No payment method is charged until the trial period concludes, and customers may cancel at any time during the trial without incurring any fees.

Automatic Renewal: After the trial period expires, eligible subscriptions are renewed automatically according to the selected billing plan. Renewal occurs on the same calendar day each month (or year, for annual plans) and continues unless the customer cancels at least three (3) business days before the renewal date. Customers are notified by email seven (7) days before each automatic renewal.

Billing Cycles and Payment Methods: Subscriptions may be billed monthly or annually. Annual plans receive a fifteen percent (15%) discount relative to the equivalent monthly plan. Accepted payment methods include major credit cards, ACH direct debit, and approved purchase orders for enterprise accounts. Invoices are generated at the start of each billing cycle and are payable within fifteen (15) days.

Cancellation Policy: Customers may cancel their subscription at any time through the billing portal or by contacting support. Cancellation takes effect at the end of the current billing period, and access to paid features continues until that date. Where a subscription is cancelled mid-cycle, no partial-month refund is issued for the unused portion.

Refunds and Disputes: Refunds are available within fourteen (14) days of the initial paid charge if the customer has not materially used the service. Refunds are not provided for subsequent renewal charges or for usage-based add-ons. Billing disputes must be raised in writing within thirty (30) days of the invoice date and are reviewed by the Finance Operations team.

Authentication and Session Management — Overview: The platform uses JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for stateless authentication across all public and internal APIs. Upon successful credential validation, the identity service issues a short-lived access token and a longer-lived refresh token, both of which are signed with the RSA private key of the authentication service.

Token Types and Lifetimes: Access tokens carry a compact set of claims including subject, roles, and scopes, and expire after fifteen (15) minutes to limit the blast radius of a leaked token. Refresh tokens have a seven (7) day time-to-live and are stored in an HttpOnly, Secure cookie to protect against cross-site scripting attacks. Refresh tokens are rotated on every use, and a reused refresh token immediately invalidates the entire session family.

Session Expiration and Invalidation: When an access token expires, the client uses its refresh token to obtain a new access token without re-authenticating. If the refresh token is expired, revoked, or absent, the server returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized and the client redirects the user to the login page. On logout, the server places the refresh token identifier into a Redis-backed revocation list so that the token cannot be reused before its natural expiry.

Password and Credential Security: Passwords are hashed with Argon2id using a per-user random salt and a memory-hard cost parameter. Failed login attempts are rate limited per account and per IP address, and the account is temporarily locked after ten consecutive failures. Multi-factor authentication via time-based one-time passwords is required for administrator roles and is strongly recommended for all other users.

Authorization and Scopes: Access tokens embed fine-grained scopes that are evaluated by an authorization middleware before each protected route handler executes. Role-based access control maps roles to permission sets, and any missing scope results in HTTP 403 Forbidden. All authorization decisions are logged to the audit trail for compliance review.

PostgreSQL Performance and Indexing — Overview: This guide describes how to diagnose and resolve slow query performance in PostgreSQL databases. It covers query instrumentation, index design, execution-plan analysis, and connection management for high-throughput production workloads.

Diagnosing Slow Queries: Enable the pg_stat_statements extension to capture aggregated execution statistics for every query. Queries whose mean execution time exceeds one hundred (100) milliseconds should be reviewed against their EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan. Look for sequential scans on large tables, high row-estimate errors, and nested loops that process far more rows than necessary.

Index Design and Optimization: Adding composite B-Tree indexes on heavily filtered columns eliminates sequential table scans and dramatically reduces CPU and I/O overhead. Place equality-filtered columns before range-filtered columns in the index definition, and consider partial indexes for queries that always filter on a status flag. Regularly run REINDEX CONCURRENTLY to counter index bloat, and use covering indexes with INCLUDE columns to enable index-only scans.

Query Planning and Statistics: The planner relies on table statistics gathered by autovacuum. Increase the statistics target for columns with skewed distributions so the planner estimates cardinality accurately. Where the planner repeatedly chooses a poor plan, consider extended statistics or a targeted hint via geqo settings. Always validate plan changes against a production-like dataset before rollout.

Connection Pooling and Concurrency: Opening a new PostgreSQL connection is expensive, so production deployments should funnel application traffic through a pooler such as PgBouncer in transaction mode. Size the pool so that active connections never exceed the database's max_connections limit, and monitor pool wait time as a leading indicator of saturation. Long-running transactions should be avoided because they block vacuum and cause table bloat.

Vacuum, Maintenance, and Monitoring: Autovacuum must be tuned so that dead tuples are reclaimed promptly and transaction ID wraparound is avoided. Monitor pg_stat_activity for blocking locks, and set statement_timeout to cap runaway queries. Track cache hit ratio, index hit ratio, and replication lag as core health metrics on the operations dashboard.

Redis Caching and Rate Limiting — Overview: The platform uses Redis as its primary in-memory datastore for caching, distributed rate limiting, and ephemeral session state. This document describes the caching strategy, eviction policies, and the rate-limiting implementation used at the API gateway.

Caching Strategy: Frequently accessed data such as user profiles, feature flags, and catalogue metadata is cached in Redis using a cache-aside pattern. Each entry is written with a time-to-live of five (5) minutes, after which it is refreshed lazily on the next read. Write-through invalidation ensures that stale entries are evicted immediately whenever the underlying record is updated, preventing outdated reads.

Eviction and Memory Management: Under high memory pressure, Redis applies the volatile-lru eviction policy so that only keys with an expiry are candidates for eviction, protecting persistent data. The maximum memory limit is configured to leave headroom for the operating system, and memory fragmentation is monitored via the INFO memory command. Hot keys are detected and, where necessary, sharded across multiple instances.

Rate Limiting with Token Buckets: The API gateway enforces a limit of one hundred (100) requests per minute per client IP address using a Redis-backed token bucket algorithm. Each request atomically decrements the bucket, and requests that exceed the limit receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header specifying the wait interval in seconds. Authenticated users may be granted higher tiers according to their plan.

Distributed Locking and Idempotency: Short-lived distributed locks are implemented with the SET NX PX command and a unique token value, guaranteeing that only one worker performs a critical section at a time. Idempotency keys are stored in Redis with a twenty-four (24) hour expiry so that duplicate payment or provisioning requests return the original result instead of executing twice.

High Availability and Persistence: Redis is deployed in a primary-replica configuration with automatic failover managed by Sentinel. AOF persistence with every-second fsync provides a balance between durability and throughput. Clients connect through a pooled connection with health checks, and cache misses degrade gracefully to the primary datastore rather than failing the request.

Parent-Document RAG — Overview: Parent-Document RAG separates the retrieval unit from the generation context. Instead of embedding large chunks directly, the system builds a two-level hierarchy of large parent chunks and small child chunks, embedding only the children for retrieval. When a child matches a query, the system uses its parent reference to retrieve the full parent, which is supplied to the LLM as complete context.

The Chunking Tradeoff: Small chunks offer precise semantic matching and reduce irrelevant information, but they can lose the surrounding context needed to interpret a statement correctly. Large chunks preserve context but dilute the embedding with unrelated information, degrading retrieval precision. Parent-Document RAG resolves this tension by searching small and generating large, so each layer uses the granularity it needs.

Parent and Child Hierarchy: A raw document is first split into parent chunks of roughly one thousand to two thousand tokens, aligned to coherent sections. Each parent is then split into child chunks of roughly two hundred tokens. Every child carries a parentId and documentId so its parent can be located exactly. The parent store holds the large contexts, while the vector index holds only the embedded children.

Retrieval and Parent Resolution: At query time the query is embedded and the child index is searched to obtain the top-K matching children. The system extracts the unique parentIds from those hits, fetches the corresponding parent chunks, and deduplicates them so that multiple matching children mapping to the same parent do not insert that parent twice. The resolved parents become the generation context.

Hybrid Retrieval and Reranking: Child retrieval need not rely on dense vectors alone. Combining dense vector search with BM25 sparse search improves recall for technical terms, product identifiers, error codes, and legal language. A cross-encoder reranker then reorders the child candidates against the original query before parent resolution, so the most relevant parents survive truncation.

Context Budgeting and Production Concerns: Because several children can map to a single large parent, the resolved context can grow quickly. Production systems therefore deduplicate parents, cap the maximum number of parents, and enforce a token budget before calling the LLM. Optional context compression and careful chunk sizing further control cost and latency. Parent-Document RAG is a relatively simple hierarchical retrieval pattern and is the foundation for the more general multi-level Hierarchical RAG approach.
